Aerosol Optical Thickness (AOT) Anomaly Detection Using Sentinel-2

records.content:
During the COVID-19 crisis parts of the world were more or less locked up at home. The hypothesis is that these social distancing measures impact aerosol amounts in the troposphere. During the sen2cor (

https://​earth​.esa​.int​/web​/sentinel​/technical​-guides​/sentinel​-2​-msi​/level​-2a​/algorithm) atmospheric correction and preprocessing of Sentinel-2 the aerosol amount is calculated as the dimensionless aerosol optical thickness (AOT). We use this data from computing temporal AOT medians on a Sentinel-2 stack from a baseline period and from the lockdown period, since the AOT is spatially and temporally highly variable. The reference period must be the same season from previous year. This script covers the respective period from 2017, 2018 and 2019. Finally, the percentage AOT difference is calculated. We call this difference the ‘COVID-19 AOT anomaly’.

def remove_and_interpolate_outliers(df):
    import pandas as pd
    import numpy as np
    # Read stats file
    
    # create thresholds
    min_threshold, max_threshold = df['mean_gamma0'].quantile([0.01,0.99])
    
    # create a new dataframe excluding the outlier rows
    outlier_removed = df[(df['mean_gamma0'] < max_threshold)&(df['mean_gamma0'] > min_threshold)]
    outliersId = df[(df['mean_gamma0'] >= max_threshold) | (df['mean_gamma0'] <= min_threshold)].index
    
    # diplay the shape of new dataset
    print(outlier_removed.shape)
    # the orignal shape 
    print(df.shape)
    
    df2=df.copy()
    # fill with nans
    df2.loc[outliersId,['mean_gamma0']]=np.nan
    # interpolate nans
    outlier_rem_interp = df2.copy()
    outlier_rem_interp['mean_gamma0'] = df2['mean_gamma0'].interpolate(method='nearest')
    return outlier_rem_interp

# utility function to read json payload into a dataframe
def stats_to_df(stats_data):
    """Transform Statistical API response into a pandas.DataFrame"""
    df_data = []

    for single_data in stats_data["data"]:
        df_entry = {}
        is_valid_entry = True

        df_entry["interval_from"] = parse_time(single_data["interval"]["from"]).date()
        df_entry["interval_to"] = parse_time(single_data["interval"]["to"]).date()

        for output_name, output_data in single_data["outputs"].items():
            for band_name, band_values in output_data["bands"].items():
                band_stats = band_values["stats"]
                if band_stats["sampleCount"] == band_stats["noDataCount"]:
                    is_valid_entry = False
                    break

                for stat_name, value in band_stats.items():
                    col_name = f"{output_name}_{band_name}_{stat_name}"
                    if stat_name == "percentiles":
                        for perc, perc_val in value.items():
                            perc_col_name = f"{col_name}_{perc}"
                            df_entry[perc_col_name] = perc_val
                    else:
                        df_entry[col_name] = value

        if is_valid_entry:
            df_data.append(df_entry)

    return pd.DataFrame(df_data)


# utility function to log training progress
def define_logger(logger_name) -> logging.Logger:
    logger = logging.getLogger(logger_name)
    logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    formatter = logging.Formatter("[%(asctime)s] {%(filename)s:%(lineno)d} %(levelname)s - %(message)s")

    stdout_handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    stdout_handler.setFormatter(formatter)
    logger.addHandler(stdout_handler)
    return logger

import numpy as np



def plot_confusion_matrix(cm,
                          target_names,
                          title='Confusion matrix',
                          cmap=None,
                          normalize=True):
    """
    given a sklearn confusion matrix (cm), make a nice plot

    Arguments
    ---------
    cm:           confusion matrix from sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix

    target_names: given classification classes such as [0, 1, 2]
                  the class names, for example: ['high', 'medium', 'low']

    title:        the text to display at the top of the matrix

    cmap:         the gradient of the values displayed from matplotlib.pyplot.cm
                  see http://matplotlib.org/examples/color/colormaps_reference.html
                  plt.get_cmap('jet') or plt.cm.Blues

    normalize:    If False, plot the raw numbers
                  If True, plot the proportions

    Usage
    -----
    plot_confusion_matrix(cm           = cm,                  # confusion matrix created by
                                                              # sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix
                          normalize    = True,                # show proportions
                          target_names = y_labels_vals,       # list of names of the classes
                          title        = best_estimator_name) # title of graph

    Citiation
    ---------
    http://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_confusion_matrix.html

    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np
    import itertools

    accuracy = np.trace(cm) / np.sum(cm).astype('float')
    misclass = 1 - accuracy

    if cmap is None:
        cmap = plt.get_cmap('Blues')

    plt.figure(figsize=(20, 20))
    plt.imshow(cm, interpolation='nearest', cmap=cmap)

    if target_names is not None:
        tick_marks = np.arange(len(target_names))
        plt.xticks(tick_marks, target_names, rotation=90)
        plt.yticks(tick_marks, target_names)

    if normalize:
        cm = cm.astype('float') / cm.sum(axis=1)[:, np.newaxis]


    thresh = np.nanmax(cm) / 1.5 if normalize else np.nanmax(cm) / 2
    for i, j in itertools.product(range(cm.shape[0]), range(cm.shape[1])):
        if normalize:
            plt.text(j, i, "{:0.2f}".format(cm[i, j]),
                     horizontalalignment="center",
                     color="white" if cm[i, j] > thresh else "black")
        else:
            plt.text(j, i, "{:,}".format(cm[i, j]),
                     horizontalalignment="center",
                     color="white" if cm[i, j] > thresh else "black")


    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.ylabel('True label')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted label\naccuracy={:0.2f}; misclass={:0.2f}'.format(accuracy, misclass))
    plt.show()




predictions, targets, polygon_ids, logprobabilities = test(lstm, val_loader)



cm = confusion_matrix(targets, predictions, labels=list(crop_id_to_label_mapping.values()))



plot_confusion_matrix(cm, target_names=[crop_id_to_name_mapping[x] for x in crop_id_to_label_mapping.keys()])

Define the API endpoints

The EOAPI is a combination of two components.

Data catalog - the

Define a function that takes the following params:

Using the /cog/statistics/ endpoint of the raster API, we get back the statistics of the item (which corresponds to one COG file) within the given geojson AOI.

The statistics includes min, max, mean, std, etc.

# the bounding box should be passed to the geojson param as a geojson Feature or FeatureCollection
def generate_stats(item, geojson):
    result = requests.post(
        f"{RASTER_API_URL}/cog/statistics", 
        params={
            "url": item.assets["cog_default"].href
        },
        json=geojson
    ).json()
    return {
        **result["properties"],
        "start_datetime": str(item.properties.get("datetime", item.properties.get("start_datetime")))[:4],
        "collection": item.collection_id
    }



Let’s start out with the US 🇺🇸 !

We’ll get all the items in the NO2 and SO2 collections and generate the statistics from them for the Ohio River Valley region of the United States.

Create a function that takes the statistics (which is a json) and converts it to a pandas dataframe in a format that’ll make it easy to read and visualize.

We are only concerned with the mean statistics for this example. Specifically the change from the year 2005 as a percentage. We’ll use pandas to calculate this change percentage and assign it to the change column.

def clean_stats(stats_json) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # convert the stats_json as is to pandas dataframe
    df = pd.json_normalize(stats_json)
    # simple renaming for readability
    df.columns = [col.replace("statistics.b1.", "") for col in df.columns]
    # create a date column from the start_datetime column
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["start_datetime"], format="mixed")
    # rename the collection to a more friendly name
    df["collection"] = df["collection"].map(lambda x: next(key for key, value in collections.items() if value == x))
    # sort the dataframe by the date column
    df = df.sort_values(by=["date"])
    # create a change column that calculates the change of the mean values from the value in 2005
    df["change"] = df.groupby("collection", group_keys=False)["mean"].apply(lambda x: x.div(x.iloc[0]).subtract(1).mul(100))
    return df

Displays a local Zarr v3 GeoZarr store (consolidated zarr.json with spatial:bbox and proj:code).
Convert a Zarr v2 store first:python convert_zarr.py ~/bucket/input_v2.zarr ~/bucket/output_v3.zarr          # EPSG read from the store
python convert_zarr.py ~/bucket/input_v2.zarr ~/bucket/output_v3.zarr --epsg 4326  # if it is not

# ==============================================================================
# 0. Start CORS & Local Zarr Proxy (works locally and on EOXHub / JupyterHub)
# ==============================================================================
# - Remote CloudFerro S3 GeoZarrs need CORS headers on HEAD requests.
# - Local cluster Zarr v2/v3 stores (e.g. `bucket/mediterranean_fronts_v3.zarr`)
#   cannot be served via Jupyter's `/files/` route because `ContentsManager`
#   blocks hidden dot-files (`.zmetadata`, `.zgroup`, `.zarray`, `.zattrs`).
# - `cors_proxy.py` handles both: upstream S3 paths (`/...`) and cluster-local
#   files (`/local/...`, with dot-files + HTTP Range/HEAD support).
# - On EOXHub, browser requests reach `127.0.0.1:8010` inside the pod through
#   `jupyter-server-proxy` at `<HUB_ORIGIN><JUPYTERHUB_SERVICE_PREFIX>proxy/8010`.

import http.client
import json
import os
import socket
import subprocess
import sys
import time

PROXY_PORT = 8010
HUB_ORIGIN = os.environ.get("HUB_ORIGIN", "https://jupyterhub.hub-otc-sc.eox.at").rstrip("/")
service_prefix = os.environ.get("JUPYTERHUB_SERVICE_PREFIX")

# Serve `/local/...` from the Jupyter Server root / $HOME (matching Jupyter's `/files/` root)
# so notebooks inside subfolders (e.g. `~/ocean_hackathon/4_Visualizations`) can still read `~/bucket/...`.
_home = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser("~"))
_cwd = os.path.abspath(os.getcwd())
LOCAL_ROOT = os.path.abspath(
    os.environ.get("JUPYTER_SERVER_ROOT")
    or (_home if os.path.commonpath([_home, _cwd]) == _home else _cwd)
)

if service_prefix:
    PROXY_BASE = f"{HUB_ORIGIN}/{service_prefix.strip('/')}/proxy/{PROXY_PORT}"
else:
    PROXY_BASE = f"http://localhost:{PROXY_PORT}"


def _check_proxy_health(port: int):
    try:
        conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", port, timeout=3)
        conn.request("GET", "/healthz")
        resp = conn.getresponse()
        body = resp.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        conn.close()
        if resp.status == 200:
            data = json.loads(body)
            if "local_root" in data:
                return data
    except Exception:
        pass
    return None


with socket.socket() as s:
    port_in_use = s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT)) == 0

health = _check_proxy_health(PROXY_PORT) if port_in_use else None

# Restart cors_proxy.py if an older instance lacks `/local/` or was started with a different `--local-root`
if port_in_use and (
    health is None or os.path.abspath(health.get("local_root", "")) != LOCAL_ROOT
):
    if "proxy" in globals() and proxy.poll() is None:
        proxy.terminate()
        proxy.wait(timeout=5)
    else:
        subprocess.run(
            ["pkill", "-f", f"cors_proxy.py.*--port {PROXY_PORT}"],
            check=False,
        )
    for _ in range(20):
        with socket.socket() as s:
            if s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT)) != 0:
                port_in_use = False
                health = None
                break
        time.sleep(0.1)

if not port_in_use:
    proxy = subprocess.Popen(
        [
            sys.executable,
            "cors_proxy.py",
            "--port",
            str(PROXY_PORT),
            "--local-root",
            LOCAL_ROOT,
        ]
    )
    for _ in range(30):
        health = _check_proxy_health(PROXY_PORT)
        if health is not None:
            break
        time.sleep(0.1)
    print(f"Started CORS & Local Zarr proxy on 127.0.0.1:{PROXY_PORT} (pid {proxy.pid})")
elif health is not None:
    print(f"Proxy already running on 127.0.0.1:{PROXY_PORT}")
else:
    print(
        f"WARNING: Port {PROXY_PORT} is occupied by another process. "
        "Stop that process or change PROXY_PORT above."
    )

# --- Diagnostic Checks ---
if health:
    print(f"  [OK] Internal health check : {health}")
try:
    conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT, timeout=5)
    conn.request("HEAD", "/EarthCODE/OSCAssets/med_cubes/ocean-med-biophysics.zarr/.zmetadata")
    up_resp = conn.getresponse()
    up_resp.read()
    conn.close()
    print(f"  [OK] Upstream S3 HEAD test : HTTP {up_resp.status} (CORS header: {up_resp.getheader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin')})")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"  [WARN] Upstream S3 check failed: {exc}")

print(f"\nBrowser Proxy Base URL: {PROXY_BASE}")
if service_prefix:
    print(f"Test EOXHub browser routing by opening: {PROXY_BASE}/healthz")



# ==============================================================================
# 1. Local Cluster Zarr v3 GeoZarr Store (via /local/ proxy route)
# ==============================================================================
# This cell only accepts EOxElements-compatible Zarr v3 stores: consolidated
# `zarr.json` with `spatial:bbox` and `proj:code` root attributes.
# Convert a Zarr v2 store first with:
#     python convert_zarr.py ~/bucket/input_v2.zarr ~/bucket/output_v3.zarr [--epsg 4326]

import importlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import ipyeoxelements
import ipyeoxelements.generated

# Reload module if EOxTimecontrol template was already patched in a prior run
if "eox-timecontrol-date" in ipyeoxelements.EOxTimecontrol._esm_template:
    importlib.reload(ipyeoxelements.generated)
    importlib.reload(ipyeoxelements)

from ipyeoxelements import EOxMap, EOxLayercontrol, EOxTimecontrol
from ipywidgets import HBox, Layout, VBox

# Path to the Zarr v3 store (relative to $HOME / Jupyter root, the current folder, or absolute)
local_zarr_rel = "bucket/mediterranean_fronts_v3.zarr"
# Variable shown first; None picks the first one. All variables can be switched in the layer control.
variable = None

_home = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser("~"))
_cwd = os.path.abspath(os.getcwd())
_local_root = globals().get("LOCAL_ROOT") or os.path.abspath(
    os.environ.get("JUPYTER_SERVER_ROOT")
    or (_home if os.path.commonpath([_home, _cwd]) == _home else _cwd)
)


def _resolve_local_zarr(zarr_path: str, local_root: str) -> tuple[Path, str]:
    """Find the store in cwd, its parent folders, LOCAL_ROOT or $HOME; return (path, URL path under /local/)."""
    root_abs = os.path.abspath(local_root)
    zarr_path = os.path.expanduser(zarr_path)
    rel_clean = zarr_path.lstrip("/")

    search_bases = []
    cur = os.path.abspath(os.getcwd())
    while True:
        search_bases.append(cur)
        if cur == root_abs or os.path.dirname(cur) == cur:
            break
        cur = os.path.dirname(cur)
    for extra in (root_abs, _home):
        if extra not in search_bases:
            search_bases.append(extra)

    candidates = []
    for base in search_bases:
        cand = os.path.abspath(zarr_path if os.path.isabs(zarr_path) else os.path.join(base, rel_clean))
        if cand not in candidates:
            candidates.append(cand)

    for cand in candidates:
        if os.path.isdir(cand):
            if os.path.commonpath([root_abs, cand]) != root_abs:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Found '{cand}', but the proxy only serves files under '{root_abs}'. "
                    "Move the store there or set LOCAL_ROOT in the proxy cell to a parent folder."
                )
            print(f"  [OK] Resolved local store: {cand}")
            return Path(cand), os.path.relpath(cand, root_abs).replace(os.sep, "/")

    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Zarr store '{zarr_path}' not found. Checked:\n" + "\n".join(f"  - {c}" for c in candidates)
    )


def _read_geozarr_v3(store_path: Path) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    """Validate an EOxElements-compatible Zarr v3 store; return (root attributes, {variable: array metadata})."""
    hint = f"Convert it with:  python convert_zarr.py {store_path} <output.zarr> [--epsg CODE]"
    root_json = store_path / "zarr.json"
    if not root_json.is_file():
        if (store_path / ".zgroup").is_file() or (store_path / ".zmetadata").is_file():
            raise ValueError(f"'{store_path}' is a Zarr v2 store; only Zarr v3 is supported here.\n{hint}")
        raise ValueError(f"'{store_path}' has no zarr.json, so it is not a Zarr v3 store.\n{hint}")

    root = json.loads(root_json.read_text())
    attrs = root.get("attributes", {})
    meta = (root.get("consolidated_metadata") or {}).get("metadata")
    missing = [k for k in ("spatial:bbox", "proj:code") if k not in attrs]
    if root.get("zarr_format") != 3 or root.get("node_type") != "group":
        raise ValueError(f"'{store_path}' root is not a Zarr v3 group.\n{hint}")
    if missing or not meta:
        problems = ([f"missing root attributes {missing}"] if missing else []) + (
            ["no consolidated metadata"] if not meta else []
        )
        raise ValueError(f"'{store_path}' is not EOxElements-compatible ({', '.join(problems)}).\n{hint}")

    y_dim, x_dim = attrs.get("spatial:dimensions", [None, None])
    variables = {}
    for name, m in meta.items():
        dims = m.get("dimension_names") or []
        if m.get("node_type") != "array" or "/" in name or len(dims) < 2:
            continue
        if y_dim and (y_dim not in dims or x_dim not in dims):
            continue
        variables[name] = m
    if not variables:
        raise ValueError(f"'{store_path}' has no 2-D (or higher) data variables to display.")
    print(
        f"  [OK] Zarr v3 GeoZarr | {attrs['proj:code']} | bbox {attrs['spatial:bbox']} | "
        f"variables: {list(variables)}"
    )
    return attrs, variables


resolved_store_path, resolved_url_rel = _resolve_local_zarr(local_zarr_rel, _local_root)
store_attrs, store_variables = _read_geozarr_v3(resolved_store_path)

if variable is None:
    variable = next(iter(store_variables))
elif variable not in store_variables:
    raise ValueError(f"Variable '{variable}' is not in the store. Choose one of: {list(store_variables)}")

if store_attrs["proj:code"] not in ("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:3857"):
    print(
        f"  [WARN] {store_attrs['proj:code']} is not built into OpenLayers; the layer may not display "
        "unless that projection is registered on the map (see polar.ipynb)."
    )

# Verify running proxy's local_root matches _local_root
if "_check_proxy_health" in globals():
    _h = _check_proxy_health(PROXY_PORT)
    if _h and os.path.abspath(_h.get("local_root", "")) != _local_root:
        print(
            f"  [WARN] Running proxy serves '{_h.get('local_root')}' instead of '{_local_root}'. "
            "Re-run the proxy cell first so `/local/` can reach this store!"
        )

# Served through cors_proxy.py's `/local/` route (HTTP Range/HEAD support behind jupyter-server-proxy)
data = f"{PROXY_BASE}/local/{resolved_url_rel}"
print("Local GeoZarr URL:", data)

# Start the colour scale on the variable's value range (written by convert_zarr.py as actual_range)
_var_attrs = store_variables[variable].get("attributes", {})
_range = _var_attrs.get("valid_range") or _var_attrs.get("actual_range") or [0, 1]
style_min, style_max = float(_range[0]), float(_range[1])
print(f"Initial variable: {variable} | colour range [{style_min:.6g}, {style_max:.6g}]")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Layer Configurations (EOxElements layer JSON, written as Python dicts)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
layers = [
    {"type": "Tile", "source": {"type": "OSM"}},
    {
        "type": "WebGLTile",
        "properties": {
            "id": "local-geozarr",
            "title": resolved_store_path.stem,
            "layerControlExpand": True,
            "layerControlToolsExpand": True,
            "layerConfig": {
                "type": "style",
                "style": True,
                "autofill": True,
            },
        },
        "source": {
            "type": "GeoZarr",
            "crossOrigin": "anonymous",
            "url": data,
            "bands": [variable],
        },
        "style": {
            "variables": {
                "min": style_min,
                "max": style_max,
            },
            "color": [
                "interpolate",
                ["linear"],
                ["band", 1],
                ["var", "min"],
                ["color", 0, 210, 255, ["band", 2]],
                [

# ==============================================================================
# - Remote CloudFerro S3 GeoZarrs need CORS headers on HEAD requests.
# - Local cluster Zarr v2/v3 stores (e.g. `bucket/mediterranean_fronts_v3.zarr`)
#   cannot be served via Jupyter's `/files/` route because `ContentsManager`
#   blocks hidden dot-files (`.zmetadata`, `.zgroup`, `.zarray`, `.zattrs`).
# - `cors_proxy.py` handles both: upstream S3 paths (`/...`) and cluster-local
#   files (`/local/...`, with dot-files + HTTP Range/HEAD support).
# - On EOXHub, browser requests reach `127.0.0.1:8010` inside the pod through
#   `jupyter-server-proxy` at `<HUB_ORIGIN><JUPYTERHUB_SERVICE_PREFIX>proxy/8010`.

import http.client
import json
import os
import socket
import subprocess
import sys
import time

PROXY_PORT = 8010
HUB_ORIGIN = os.environ.get("HUB_ORIGIN", "https://jupyterhub.hub-otc-sc.eox.at").rstrip("/")
service_prefix = os.environ.get("JUPYTERHUB_SERVICE_PREFIX")

# Serve `/local/...` from the Jupyter Server root / $HOME (matching Jupyter's `/files/` root)
# so notebooks inside subfolders (e.g. `~/ocean_hackathon/4_Visualizations`) can still read `~/bucket/...`.
_home = os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser("~"))
_cwd = os.path.abspath(os.getcwd())
LOCAL_ROOT = os.path.abspath(
    os.environ.get("JUPYTER_SERVER_ROOT")
    or (_home if os.path.commonpath([_home, _cwd]) == _home else _cwd)
)

if service_prefix:
    PROXY_BASE = f"{HUB_ORIGIN}/{service_prefix.strip('/')}/proxy/{PROXY_PORT}"
else:
    PROXY_BASE = f"http://localhost:{PROXY_PORT}"


def _check_proxy_health(port: int):
    try:
        conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", port, timeout=3)
        conn.request("GET", "/healthz")
        resp = conn.getresponse()
        body = resp.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        conn.close()
        if resp.status == 200:
            data = json.loads(body)
            if "local_root" in data:
                return data
    except Exception:
        pass
    return None


with socket.socket() as s:
    port_in_use = s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT)) == 0

health = _check_proxy_health(PROXY_PORT) if port_in_use else None

# Restart cors_proxy.py if an older instance lacks `/local/` or was started with a different `--local-root`
if port_in_use and (
    health is None or os.path.abspath(health.get("local_root", "")) != LOCAL_ROOT
):
    if "proxy" in globals() and proxy.poll() is None:
        proxy.terminate()
        proxy.wait(timeout=5)
    else:
        subprocess.run(
            ["pkill", "-f", f"cors_proxy.py.*--port {PROXY_PORT}"],
            check=False,
        )
    for _ in range(20):
        with socket.socket() as s:
            if s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT)) != 0:
                port_in_use = False
                health = None
                break
        time.sleep(0.1)

if not port_in_use:
    proxy = subprocess.Popen(
        [
            sys.executable,
            "cors_proxy.py",
            "--port",
            str(PROXY_PORT),
            "--local-root",
            LOCAL_ROOT,
        ]
    )
    for _ in range(30):
        health = _check_proxy_health(PROXY_PORT)
        if health is not None:
            break
        time.sleep(0.1)
    print(f"Started CORS & Local Zarr proxy on 127.0.0.1:{PROXY_PORT} (pid {proxy.pid})")
elif health is not None:
    print(f"Proxy already running on 127.0.0.1:{PROXY_PORT}")
else:
    print(
        f"WARNING: Port {PROXY_PORT} is occupied by another process. "
        "Stop that process or change PROXY_PORT above."
    )

# --- Diagnostic Checks ---
if health:
    print(f"  [OK] Internal health check : {health}")
try:
    conn = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", PROXY_PORT, timeout=5)
    conn.request("HEAD", "/EarthCODE/OSCAssets/med_cubes/ocean-med-biophysics.zarr/.zmetadata")
    up_resp = conn.getresponse()
    up_resp.read()
    conn.close()
    print(f"  [OK] Upstream S3 HEAD test : HTTP {up_resp.status} (CORS header: {up_resp.getheader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin')})")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"  [WARN] Upstream S3 check failed: {exc}")

print(f"\nBrowser Proxy Base URL: {PROXY_BASE}")
if service_prefix:
    print(f"Test EOXHub browser routing by opening: {PROXY_BASE}/healthz")

The EDC (Euro Data Cube) workspace provides Dask Gateway for scalable analysis of collections that are larger than memory. This notebook starts with a local Dask client and uses the 4DMED-SEA sea-surface salinity collection as an ocean example.

The same workflow can then be moved to the Dask Gateway provided by EDC.

import xarray as xr
from dask.distributed import Client

Dask extends familiar Python array and dataframe libraries with lazy, parallel execution. Xarray can represent a large remote array as many smaller chunks and build a task graph before any values are loaded. Computation begins only when an operation such as compute(), load(), or plotting requests a result.

This separation between describing and executing a workflow lets you inspect the planned work, select only the required data, and scale from a laptop to a distributed cluster with few code changes.

A generic example of task graphs and worker scheduling:

A local client is sufficient for learning, developing a workflow, and testing small selections. The client also provides a Dask Dashboard link for inspecting tasks, memory, and worker activity.

client = Client()
client

Please don’t run this during the main sessions. If many people start clusters together during the workshop, the auto-scaler will take quite a bit of time to create new workers.

The following Zarr store contains Mediterranean sea-surface salinity and density fields. Passing chunks={} keeps the arrays lazy so opening the collection reads metadata rather than loading the full dataset.

from pystac_client import Client as STACClient

catalog = STACClient.open("https://eoapi.workspace.earthcode.eox.at/stac/")
item = next(catalog.search(collections=["4dmed-2d-sss"]).items())
item



item.assets["data"].href



dataset = xr.open_zarr(item.assets["data"].href, chunks={})
dataset

Select one date and the surface layer, then coarsen the spatial grid. These operations construct a task graph without immediately downloading all source chunks.

salinity = dataset["sos"].sel(
    time="2020-06-15",
    depth=0,
    method="nearest",
    drop=True,
)

plot_data = salinity.coarsen(
    lat=4,
    lon=4,
    boundary="trim",
).mean()

plot_data.data



plot_data.data.visualize(optimize_graph=True)

Calling compute() executes the graph and returns the selected result to the notebook. Watch the Dask Dashboard while this cell runs to see tasks move through the scheduler and workers.

Use JupyterLab’s Dask sidebar to open panels such as Graph, Progress, Task Stream, and Workers Memory:

computed = plot_data.compute()
computed.plot(cmap="viridis")

Close clients and clusters when you finish so their resources are available to other work.

client.close()

This repository contains information and guided notebooks about the Ocean Hackathon. The core aspects of the hackathon are:

Marine datasets covering the Mediterranean Sea and the global ocean from ESA-funded science projects, hosted on object storage.

A Mediterranean Sea datacube with a common spatial grid and separate stores for monthly, hourly, and daily data.

Guided notebooks that show how to access the cloud-hosted datasets, convert data into cloud-native formats, combine them into analysis-ready datacubes, and use those collections in scientific workflows.

The 

ESA Mediterranean Sea Datacube combines marine datasets on a common 1/24° EPSG:4326 grid. The data are available in four online GeoZarr stores with different time and depth coordinates:

Store

Contents

Cube coordinate coverage

ocean​-med​-monthly​-cube​.zarr

4DMED PFT/Kd, ocean heat content, OceanSODA, BICEP, and MITHO

Monthly, January 2016–December 2022

hourly_cube.zarr

WOC and CMEMS current components at 15 m

Hourly, 30 December 2014–30 December 2019

ocean​-med​-biophysics​.zarr

4DMED primary production and 3D physical fields at 18 depths, 3–135 m

Daily, 1 January 2016–31 July 2022

ocean​-med​-daily​-surface​-cube​.zarr

4DMED salinity/density, FSLE, both 4DVarNet reconstructions, and CAREHeat categories

Daily, 1 January 2016–31 December 2022

The notebooks open these online stores directly over HTTPS using consolidated metadata. An internet connection is required; only the selected chunks are read. Group 0 is full resolution; groups 1 and 2 contain spatial summaries at 1/6° and 1/3°. Individual products may cover only part of a store’s time axis.

Start with 

cube access and example plots, then explore 

building a local cube from two datasets and 

time series at every depth. The 

overview lists source products, OSC links, variables, licences, and how the data were combined.

The format notebooks show 1) how datasets can be transformed in cloud-optimised formats, and 2) described with metadata.

Note: the examples we used for these notebooks come from Polar studies, since they came in different file formats.

Format

Best for

Why it matters in object storage

Zarr

Labelled multidimensional arrays

Chunked reads allow an analysis to load only the required variables, regions, depths, and times.

Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)

Individual rasters or raster stacks

Internal tiling and overviews support efficient range reads and quicklooks.

GeoParquet

Vector geometries and tabular observations

Columnar storage enables efficient filtering and carries standard geospatial metadata.

See the notebooks in 3_File_formats_and_metadata/ and the 

Cloud-Native Geospatial Guide for more detail.

Rich metadata makes each collection easier to find, interpret, cite, and reuse. Collection metadata should document provenance, licence, variables, units, spatial and temporal extent, processing history, and access assets.

EarthCODE collections use the 

SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) specification to provide a consistent, machine-readable description of geospatial data.

Most of the datasets are part of one of the cubes, which in turn can be interactively visualised since they are in geozarr format. To open the visualisation click the “Explore Data” link in the ntoebooks, or go directly to the visualisation 

website . The site wraps a simple GeoZarr viewer and can be replaced with a compatible GeoZarr in any programming language or tool.
Additionally, there are two notebooks if you are interested in converting your own data. They use a sample of the OceanSoda Dataset to demonstrate the conversions:

Visualising COGs

Converting Zarr to GeoZarr

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

pft_names = ["DIATO", "DINO", "GREEN", "HAPTO", "PROKA"]

pft = ds[pft_names].to_array(dim="pft")
summer = pft.sel(
    time=pft.time.dt.month.isin([6, 7, 8])
).mean("time")




total_chlorophyll is the combined chlorophyll concentration of the five groups. dominant_pft stores the index of the group with the highest concentration at each grid cell.

total_chlorophyll = summer.sum("pft", min_count=1)

dominant_pft = (
    summer.fillna(-np.inf)
    .argmax("pft")
    .where(total_chlorophyll.notnull())
)

total_chlorophyll = total_chlorophyll.compute()
dominant_pft = dominant_pft.compute()



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm

import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy.feature as cfeature

pft_colours = [
    "#d95f02",  # Diatoms
    "#7570b3",  # Dinoflagellates
    "#1b9e77",  # Green algae
    "#e6ab02",  # Haptophytes
    "#66a9c9",  # Prokaryotic phytoplankton
]

pft_labels = [
    "Diatoms",
    "Dinoflagellates",
    "Green algae",
    "Haptophytes",
    "Prokaryotic phytoplankton",
]

cmap = ListedColormap(pft_colours)
norm = BoundaryNorm(np.arange(-0.5, 5.5, 1), cmap.N)

projection = ccrs.PlateCarree()

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 7))
ax = plt.axes(projection=projection)

ax.set_extent(
    [
        float(ds.lon.min()),
        float(ds.lon.max()),
        float(ds.lat.min()),
        float(ds.lat.max()),
    ],
    crs=projection,
)

ax.pcolormesh(
    ds.lon,
    ds.lat,
    dominant_pft,
    cmap=cmap,
    norm=norm,
    shading="auto",
    transform=projection,
)


ax.add_feature(cfeature.LAND, facecolor="lightgrey", zorder=3)
ax.coastlines(resolution="50m", linewidth=0.7, zorder=4)

legend_handles = [
    mpatches.Patch(color=colour, label=label)
    for colour, label in zip(pft_colours, pft_labels)
]

ax.legend(
    handles=legend_handles,
    title="Dominant PFT",
    loc="upper left",
    frameon=True,
)

ax.set_title(
    "Dominant phytoplankton functional type and total chlorophyll\n"
    "Summer, 2019–2021"
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Here, the resolution of the dynamical model used for the learning/training (eNATL60-BLB02) is here downgraded to 1/20°. This product provides additional variables such as Absolute Dynamic Topography and geostrophic currents (both absolute values and anomalies) at a resolution of 1/24° over the Mediterranean Sea and for the period from 2016 to 2022. target_month = "2022-06"

fsle_month = ds.fsle.sel(time=target_month).compute()



strong_fsle = float(
    fsle_month.quantile(
        0.90,
        dim=("time", "y", "x"),
        skipna=True
    )
)

print(f"Monthly 90th-percentile threshold: {strong_fsle:.3f} day⁻¹")



valid_days = fsle_month.notnull().sum("time")

import cartopy.feature as cfeature


def plot_med_water_class(da, label="smoothed mode dominant water class"):

    # 14 discrete OWT classes
    classes = np.arange(1, 15)

    # A categorical colour map
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab20", 14)

    # Boundaries put each integer in the centre of a colour bin
    boundaries = np.arange(0.5, 15.5, 1)
    norm = mcolors.BoundaryNorm(
        boundaries,
        ncolors=cmap.N
    )

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 7))

    ax = plt.axes(
        projection=ccrs.PlateCarree()
    )

    im = ax.pcolormesh(
        da.lon,
        da.lat,
        da,
        cmap=cmap,
        norm=norm,
        shading="nearest",
        transform=ccrs.PlateCarree()
    )

    ax.set_extent(
        [lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max],
        crs=ccrs.PlateCarree()
    )

    ax.add_feature(
        cfeature.LAND,
        facecolor="lightgrey",
        zorder=2
    )

    ax.add_feature(
        cfeature.COASTLINE,
        linewidth=0.6,
        zorder=3
    )

    ax.add_feature(
        cfeature.BORDERS,
        linewidth=0.3,
        zorder=3
    )

    cbar = plt.colorbar(
        im,
        ax=ax,
        ticks=classes,
        boundaries=boundaries,
        pad=0.03,
        shrink=0.85
    )

    cbar.set_label(label)

    date = da.time.values if "time" in da.coords else ds.time.isel(time=time_index).values

        f"Bio-optical Seascape - Mediterranean\n"

    return fig, ax

The “date_start” and “date_end” are another key part of the data.

For example, one can compute the duration of a events at certain location by doing:

import pandas as pd

ds = xr.open_zarr(items["careheat-database-careheat_mhw_metrics_2d"].assets["data"].href)

# select all the date starts and date ends for the Med
dstart = ds["date_start"].sel(lon=slice(-6.062, 36.06), lat=slice(30.27, 45.98), drop=True)
dend = ds["date_end"].sel(lon=slice(-6.062, 36.06), lat=slice(30.27, 45.98), drop=True)



dstart.isel(nevent=0).values



keep = (dstart.values >= 20200501) & (dend.values < 20200700)




def parse_ymd(block):
    a = block.ravel()
    dates = pd.to_datetime(
        {
            "year": a // 10000,
            "month": (a // 100) % 100,
            "day": a % 100,
        },
        errors="coerce",
    )
    return dates.to_numpy(dtype="datetime64[ns]").reshape(block.shape)

def convert_dates(da):
    return xr.apply_ufunc(
        parse_ymd,
        da.where(keep),
        dask="parallelized",
        output_dtypes=[np.dtype("datetime64[ns]")],
    )

start = convert_dates(dstart)
end = convert_dates(dend)

duration_days = ((end - start) / np.timedelta64(1, "D")).rename(
    "duration_days"
)
duration_days.attrs = {"units": "days"}



start.values[0]



# duration_days already contains only events starting in June
valid = duration_days.notnull()

# First valid event index at each grid cell
first = valid.argmax(dim="nevent").compute()

# Reduce to (lat, lon); mask cells with no matching event
monthly_duration = duration_days.isel(nevent=first).where(
    valid.any(dim="nevent")
)

The MEDICANES atlas contains observations from different satellites over medicane events in Mediterranean Sea. All data are available at Ifremer : 

https://​data​-cersat​.ifremer​.fr​/data​/storms​/medicanes​/storm​-atlas/

In particular, the climatology folder contains observations from various satellite products colocated with Mediterranean storms, from 1991 to 2020. The storms are numbered from 513 (example: track00000513) to 1716 (track00001716). Each storm folder contains subfolders, for each observation product that was colocated with the storm trajectory. For instance for storm folder track00001556, the SCATSAT1-L2-ICM subfolder contains wind speed and direction by Indian scatterometer SCATSAT-1. The different passes of this satellite colocated with this storm are stored in time ordered subfolders (<year/day in the year>, for instance track00001556/SCATSAT1-L2-ICM/2017/040/

All storm trajectories are stored in the file (in parquet format): 

https://​data​-cersat​.ifremer​.fr​/data​/storms​/medicanes​/tracks​/climatology​/medicanes​_cl7​.parquet

Let’s collect for instance an observation file from SCATSAT-1 scatterometer for the storm track00001556:

This dataset provides monthly information on Cumulative Hazard Indexs (CHIs) at the sea surface (3D, lat, lon, time) at global scale. The dataset is split into 3 zarr stores:

This tutorial accesses the published Zarr stores over HTTPS and illustrates the
multistressor construction of CHI1, global July 2022 conditions, and annual changes across
the Mediterranean and four subbasins: Western Mediterranean, Adriatic, Ionian,
and Levantine–Aegean. The monthly map shows July 2022; time series cover the full record.

The Mediterranean is used here as a regional example to illustrate basin-scale and subbasin-scale analyses.
A global map provides context; basin analyses are examples, not a geographic restriction of the data.

Source: 

original NetCDF dataset on Zenodo
· 

catalogue entry
· 

MiTHo

Index

Inputs / stressors

Available period

Levels

CHI1

Sea surface temperature (SST): warm and cold extremes; hydrogen ion concentration (H+): acidification

Jan 1993–Dec 2022

Surface

CHI2

Temperature: warm and cold extremes; dissolved oxygen: deoxygenation; salinity: low and high extremes

Jan 2004–Nov 2022

2.5 dbar (level=0), 200 dbar (level=1)

CHI3

SST, H+, sea surface salinity (SSS), sea surface density (SSD), wind speed: nine stressors in total

Jan 1993–Dec 2022

Surface

CHI4

SST: warm and cold extremes; fishing effort (FE): high values

Jan 2012–Dec 2020

Surface

The dataset is gridded on a 1° x 1° regular lat-lon grid.Geographic coverage and valid-data masks differ between indices.
CHI3 combines both low and high extremes of SSS, SSD and wind in a single index.
For any given variable and threshold pair, low and high extremes are mutually exclusive
at the same place and time. Extremes of different variables can occur together.

The other stores contain CHI2 and CHI4. Fetching each store’s root metadata below
checks that all three URLs expose Zarr 3 groups, without loading their data arrays.

from pystac_client import Client

catalog = Client.open("https://eoapi.workspace.earthcode.eox.at/stac/")
collection = catalog.search(collections=["global-cumulative-hazard-indexes-chis"]).item_collection()
items = {item.id: item for item in collection}

# The three published datasets.
STORES = {
    "CHI1 / CHI3": items["global-cumulative-hazard-indexes-chis-mitho-ch13"],
    "CHI2": items["global-cumulative-hazard-indexes-chis-mitho-chi2_2004_2022"],
    "CHI4": items["global-cumulative-hazard-indexes-chis-mitho-chi4_2012_2020"],
}
collection



[item.assets["data"].href for item in collection]



Fetch the small root metadata from each store to check access. This does not download the full datasets.

# Read one metadata document per store.
store_checks = []
for label, source_item in STORES.items():
    with urllib.request.urlopen(source_item.assets["data"].href + "/zarr.json", timeout=60) as response:
        root = json.load(response)
    assert root["zarr_format"] == 3 and root["node_type"] == "group"

records.content:
The original processing code constructs the unnormalized CHI1 as:

CHI1 = S_MHW + S_CS + S_PH

S_MHW is the marine-heatwave contribution, S_CS the cold-spell contribution,
and S_PH the acidification contribution. They are non-negative, dimensionless
stressor intensities derived from standardized anomalies at detected extremes.
They are not raw SST or pH measurements. For SST, the processing uses monthly
90th/10th percentile thresholds for warm/cold extremes, respectively.

The example uses the unnormalized, fixed-climatology variables. _mav identifies
the alternative based on a moving climatology, rather than simply a smoothed CHI
time series. _norm, _mean, _std, _Cat and _PI identify other derived products;
they are not interchangeable with the variables plotted here.

Higher CHI values indicate a larger sum of stressor contributions under this method;
they are not calibrated probabilities of ecological damage. The baseline depends
on the input product and must be considered when comparing different indices.

For CHI1, _norm divides the raw index by the global spatial maximum of each month.
The global context below uses raw CHI1, not this normalized variant.

# Names and example settings can be changed here.
VARIABLES = ["CH1_CHI1", "CH1_S_MHW", "CH1_S_CS", "CH1_S_PH"]
LABELS = [
    "CHI1 — cumulative index",
    "Marine heatwave contribution",
    "Cold-spell contribution",
    "Acidification contribution",
]
assert set(VARIABLES).issubset(ds.data_vars)
assert all(ds[v].dims == ("time", "latitude", "longitude") for v in VARIABLES)

DATE = "2022-07"
MASK_FILE = Path("inputs/mediterranean_subbasin_masks_1deg.nc")
LON_BOUNDS = (-6.062, 36.06)
LAT_BOUNDS = (30.27, 45.98)



A small helper keeps geographic slicing valid for either coordinate ordering.

# Reverse the slice if coordinates run from north to south.
def coordinate_slice(coord, bounds):
    # Support both ascending and descending latitude/longitude coordinates.
    return (
        slice(*bounds) if coord.values[0] < coord.values[-1] else slice(*bounds[::-1])
    )


DYNAMIC_VARIABLES = VARIABLES + ["CH1_CHI1_norm"]



Select only the variables and geographic rectangle needed for the regional example.

# Selection is still lazy; no numerical arrays are loaded yet.
subset = ds[DYNAMIC_VARIABLES].sel(
    longitude=coordinate_slice(ds.longitude, LON_BOUNDS),
    latitude=coordinate_slice(ds.latitude, LAT_BOUNDS),
)
assert subset.sizes["latitude"] > 0 and subset.sizes["longitude"] > 0
print("Native chunks:", {v: ds[v].encoding.get("chunks") for v in VARIABLES})
print("Subset dimensions:", dict(subset.sizes))

# Read only these five variables, with bounded concurrent chunk decompression.
# Native chunks are large: a small map/point may still require substantial I/O.



Load the selected regional data once, then extract the July 2022 map.

# Limit concurrent decompression because the native chunks are large.

    regional = subset.compute()

selected_month = regional.sel(time=DATE)

snapshot = selected_month.isel(time=0, drop=True)

Use the same spatial sample in every month: only cells with finite CHI1,

Weights are proportional to cos(latitude). Missing areas are not filled or
extrapolated. The coverage table reports how much of each CHI marine footprint
is retained. Subbasin means use the supplied boundaries, not rectangular selections.

Each panel shows basin-mean CHI1 and its three contributions, on a common y scale.
The dashed line marks July 2022. All 360 monthly samples are shown without smoothing.

# Keep the same complete-data cells throughout the record.
all_complete = (
    np.isfinite(regional[DYNAMIC_VARIABLES].to_array("variable"))
    .all("variable")
    .all("time")
)
lat_weights = np.cos(np.deg2rad(regional.latitude)).broadcast_like(med_mask)
coverage_rows, basin_weights, basin_monthly_fields = [], {}, {}
monthly_frames = []



Compute one area-weighted monthly series per basin for each variable.

# Cosine latitude weights account for cell-area differences on the regular grid.
for name, mask in basin_masks.items():
    retained = mask & all_complete
    assert int(retained.sum()) > 0, f"No complete cells in {name}"
    w = lat_weights.where(retained, 0)
    basin_weights[name] = w
    fields = regional[VARIABLES].weighted(w).mean(("latitude", "longitude"))
    basin_monthly_fields[name] = fields
    coverage_rows.append(
        {
            "Basin": name,
            "CHI marine grid cells": int(mask.sum()),
            "Retained complete cells": int(retained.sum()),
            "Retained area fraction (%)": float(
                100 * w.sum() / lat_weights.where(mask, 0).sum()
            ),
        }
    )
    frame = fields.to_dataframe()[VARIABLES].reset_index()
    frame.insert(0, "Basin", name)
    monthly_frames.append(frame)



Inspect the retained coverage before interpreting the basin means.

records.content:
Keep the same spatial sample in every month: retain basin grid cells with finite
CHI1, normalized CHI1 and all three contributions for all 360 months.
Use weights proportional to cos(latitude) for the equal-angle grid. The coverage
table reports the retained fraction of each geographic mask; results describe those
observed cells, not an extrapolation to missing parts of the basin.

Three metrics separate different aspects:

Mean CHI1: mean over retained basin cells and all months of each year, including zeros.

Affected area: annual mean of the monthly area fraction satisfying CHI1_norm > 1e-4.

Intensity when active: annual weighted mean raw CHI1 across the active cell-months only.

The last metric helps separate magnitude from occurrence. An increase in mean CHI1
alone does not establish that individual extremes became stronger. These are descriptive
comparisons under a fixed-climatology index, not a trend-significance or attribution test.

# Aggregate the monthly data by calendar year; active intensity excludes inactive cell-months.
annual_rows, decade_rows = [], []
basin_monthly = {}
for name, mask in basin_masks.items():
    w = basin_weights[name]
    retained = w > 0
    total_w = w.sum()
    field = regional.CH1_CHI1.where(retained)
    active = (regional.CH1_CHI1_norm > 1e-4) & retained
    monthly_mean = field.weighted(w).mean(("latitude", "longitude"))
    active_weight = w.where(active, 0).sum(("latitude", "longitude"))
    active_sum = (field.where(active, 0) * w).sum(("latitude", "longitude"))
    monthly_fraction = 100 * active_weight / total_w
    annual_mean = monthly_mean.resample(time="YS").mean()
    annual_area = monthly_fraction.resample(time="YS").mean()
    annual_intensity = (
        active_sum.resample(time="YS").sum() / active_weight.resample(time="YS").sum()
    )
    basin_monthly[name] = {
        "mean": monthly_mean,
        "area": monthly_fraction,
        "active_sum": active_sum,
        "active_weight": active_weight,
    }
    for i, time in enumerate(annual_mean.time.values):
        annual_rows.append(
            {
                "Basin": name,
                "Year": pd.Timestamp(time).year,
                "Mean CHI1": float(annual_mean[i]),
                "Affected area (%)": float(annual_area[i]),
                "Intensity when active": float(annual_intensity[i]),
            }
        )
    for label, start, end in [
        ("1993–2002", "1993", "2002"),
        ("2013–2022", "2013", "2022"),
    ]:
        s = slice(start, end)
        decade_rows.append(
            {
                "Basin": name,
                "Period": label,
                "Mean CHI1": float(monthly_mean.sel(time=s).mean()),
                "Affected area (%)": float(monthly_fraction.sel(time=s).mean()),
                "Intensity when active": float(
                    active_sum.sel(time=s).sum() / active_weight.sel(time=s).sum()
                ),
            }
        )



Display and save the annual and first/last-decade summaries.

# The coverage table remains the reference for interpreting every mean.
annual_table = pd.DataFrame(annual_rows)
decade_table = pd.DataFrame(decade_rows)
display(coverage_table.round(2))
display(decade_table.round(3))
coverage_table.to_csv(ARTIFACTS / "basin_coverage.csv", index=False)
annual_table.to_csv(ARTIFACTS / "basin_annual_metrics.csv", index=False)
decade_table.to_csv(ARTIFACTS / "basin_decade_comparison.csv", index=False)

axes[-1].set_xlabel("Year")

fractions = {row["Basin"]: row["Retained area fraction (%)"] for row in coverage_rows}
fig.suptitle(
    "CHI1 annual evolution — Mediterranean and four subbasins\nFixed complete-data masks and area weighting",
    fontsize=13,

Compare raw mean CHI1 in 1993–2002 and 2013–2022 using the same complete-data
Mediterranean cells. Positive differences indicate larger mean cumulative intensity,
which can reflect changes in both occurrence and magnitude. No significance test is applied.

# Retain the same complete-data cells in both decades.
retained_med = med_mask & all_complete
early = (
    regional.CH1_CHI1.sel(time=slice("1993", "2002")).mean("time").where(retained_med)
)
late = (
    regional.CH1_CHI1.sel(time=slice("2013", "2022")).mean("time").where(retained_med)
)
change = late - early
common_max = max(float(early.max()), float(late.max()), 1e-12)
change_max = max(float(abs(change).max()), 1e-12)



Compare the two decade means on a shared scale and map their difference separately.

# The difference uses a symmetric diverging colour scale centred on zero.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1,
    3,
    figsize=(15, 4.2),
    subplot_kw={"projection": ccrs.PlateCarree()},
    layout="constrained",
)
for i, (ax, field, title) in enumerate(
    zip(
        axes,
        [early, late, change],
        [
            "Mean CHI1: 1993–2002",
            "Mean CHI1: 2013–2022",
            "Difference: last − first decade",
        ],
    )
):
    kwargs = (
        {"cmap": "viridis", "vmin": 0, "vmax": common_max}
        if i < 2
        else {"cmap": "RdBu_r", "vmin": -change_max, "vmax": change_max}
    )
    im = ax.pcolormesh(
        field.longitude,
        field.latitude,
        field,
        shading="auto",
        transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
        **kwargs
    )
    ax.set_extent([*LON_BOUNDS, *LAT_BOUNDS], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())

records.content:
Use the stored products, and first verify them against the monthly normalized data.
All maps cover the full 1993–2022 period:

Persistency: number of months with CHI1_norm > 1e-4.

Low Category: number of months with 0 < CHI1_norm <= 0.33.

Medium Category: number of months with 0.33 < CHI1_norm <= 0.66.

High Category: number of months with 0.66 < CHI1_norm <= 1.001.

The 1.001 upper bound is the numerical margin used in the source code; the nominal
normalized upper limit is 1. Category is relative to each month’s global spatial maximum,
not an absolute hazard threshold. Categories partition positive normalized values;
their total can differ from PI because PI excludes values at or below 1e-4.

These full-period counts locate repeated occurrence but do not themselves show
whether events increased towards the end of the record. Use the annual metrics above
for that question. Maps below retain the same complete-data Mediterranean mask.
Each panel has its own colour scale in months, to make the rarer high category visible;
compare the colourbar values, not colours alone, between panels.

# Load the supplied full-period count maps only when they are needed.
STATIC_VARIABLES = ["CH1_CHI1_PI", "CH1_CHI1_Cat"]
with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads", num_workers=2):
    static_region = (
        ds[STATIC_VARIABLES]
        .sel(latitude=regional.latitude, longitude=regional.longitude)
        .compute()
    )



Check that the supplied counts agree with the monthly normalized index.

# Count months, not consecutive duration; preserve the original category thresholds.
norm_series = regional.CH1_CHI1_norm
computed_pi = (norm_series > 1e-4).sum("time")
pi = static_region.CH1_CHI1_PI
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pi.values[retained_med.values], computed_pi.values[retained_med.values]
)
category = static_region.CH1_CHI1_Cat
assert category.sizes["intensity_class"] == 3
category_ranges = [(0, 0.33), (0.33, 0.66), (0.66, 1.001)]
for i, (lower, upper) in enumerate(category_ranges):
    recomputed = ((norm_series > lower) & (norm_series <= upper)).sum("time")
    stored = category.isel(intensity_class=i)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        stored.values[retained_med.values], recomputed.values[retained_med.values]
    )
print(
    "Stored PI and all three Category counts match monthly data on the retained Mediterranean mask."
)



Draw PI and the three categories, each with its own explicitly labelled count scale.

# Different panels have different count ranges, so compare their colourbar values.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    2,
    2,
    figsize=(13, 7),
    subplot_kw={"projection": ccrs.PlateCarree()},
    layout="constrained",
)
fields = [pi] + [category.isel(intensity_class=i) for i in range(3)]
titles = [
    "Persistency: normalized CHI1 > 10⁻⁴",
    "Low Category: (0, 0.33]",
    "Medium Category: (0.33, 0.66]",
    "High Category: (0.66, 1.001]",
]
for ax, field, title in zip(axes.flat, fields, titles):
    field = field.where(retained_med)
    im = ax.pcolormesh(
        field.longitude,
        field.latitude,
        field,
        transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
        shading="auto",
        cmap="YlOrRd",
        vmin=0,
        vmax=max(float(field.max()), 1),
    )
    ax.set_extent([*LON_BOUNDS, *LAT_BOUNDS], crs=ccrs.PlateCarree())
    ax.add_feature(cfeature.LAND.with_scale("110m"), facecolor="0.85", zorder=3)
    ax.coastlines(resolution="110m", linewidth=0.5)
    for basin_mask in submasks.values():
        ax.contour(
            basin_mask.longitude,
            basin_mask.latitude,
            basin_mask.astype(float),
            levels=[0.5],
            colors=["0.35"],
            linewidths=0.5,
            transform=ccrs.PlateCarree(),
            zorder=5,
        )
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    cb = fig.colorbar(
        im,
        ax=ax,
        orientation="horizontal",
        pad=0.05,
        shrink=0.9,
        label="Number of months (panel-specific scale)",
    )
    cb.locator = plt.MaxNLocator(nbins=5, integer=True)
    cb.update_ticks()
fig.suptitle(
    "Mediterranean CHI1 Persistency and Category, 1993–2022\nSupplied subbasin boundaries in grey",
    fontsize=14,
)
fig.savefig(
    ARTIFACTS / "chi1_mediterranean_persistency_categories.png",
    dpi=160,
    bbox_inches="tight",
)
plt.show()



Save the run settings and close the remote dataset.

# Only derived outputs are written; source archives remain unchanged.
validation.update(
    {
        "basin_masks": list(basin_masks),
        "coverage": coverage_rows,
        "pi_and_category_counts_verified": True,
        "normalization": "raw CHI1 divided by its monthly global spatial maximum",
    }
)
(ARTIFACTS / "validation.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(validation, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"

lats = ds['latitude_20Hz']

    (np.abs(lons - lon_location) < vicinity_degree)
    & (np.abs(lats - lat_location) < vicinity_degree)
).compute()

# Convert seconds since 1 Jan 2000 to datetime

    time_values,
    unit='s',
    origin='2000-01-01'
)

# Calculate mean SWH for each timestamp

The ESA Mediterranean Sea Datacube brings selected marine datasets onto a common 1/24° latitude/longitude grid (EPSG:4326) for the Mediterranean Sea.

The data are available in four online GeoZarr stores: monthly fields, hourly currents, daily surface fields, and daily biophysics. The stores share the same horizontal grid and keep the time and depth coordinates each dataset needs.

This shared grid lets you compare variables without repeating the spatial alignment.

The associated notebooks show how to:

Acces the ESA Mediterranean Sea Datacube

Build one local datacube from two datasets selects 4DMED-SEA salinity and CAREHeat categories, resamples both datasets over the Mediterranean Sea, and saves and plots the local cube.

Do larger scale analysis (Time Series at Every Depth) .

The access examples open the online GeoZarr stores linked below directly from EarthCODE object storage.

A simple visualisation of the data cube is available at 

the GeoZarr viewer:

Use the 

individual dataset notebooks to explore the source products.

All spatial layers are aligned to one EPSG:4326 lat/lon grid. Full-resolution level 0 uses 1/24° cells, with longitude centres from approximately -6.0625 to 36.0625 and latitude centres from 30.2708 to 45.9792, giving 1,012 columns by 378 rows.

Each store is a multiscale GeoZarr with groups 0, 1, and 2. These represent 1/24°, 1/6°, and 1/3° spacing, with spatial shapes 378 × 1,012, 94 × 253, and 47 × 126.

The same lat, lon position refers to the same place across every store at a given level. (The grid has different physical cell areas at different latitudes.)

Data values are spatially interpolated using nearest neighbour from the source data.

Monthly fields are averaged into calendar months and indexed by month start. Daily fields are aligned to daily timestamps.

The biophysics cube preserves 18 common depth levels from 3 to 135 m, positive down. WOC has one depth level at 15 m.

All four stores include water_mask: 1 retains water or unmapped offshore cells and 0 excludes mapped land. It comes from ESA WorldCover 2021 overviews and is applied across time and depth; The mask is not guaranteed permanent water, but rather an np.isin([0,80]) (i.e. non land and permanent water bodies) applied to the land classificaiton product.

The separate `ocean-cube.json` prototype contains `CHL3D`, `DS3D`, `SAL3D`, `TEMP3D`, `UO3D`, and `VO3D` from the 3D biophysical product. It is not the supplied `ocean-med-biophysics.zarr` store. WAPOSAL and the other catalogue products absent from the four build workflows remain available as individual datasets.

The upsampling or downsampling used to create the cubes can make the variables unsuitable for some scientific analyses. The original datasets remain available through 

1_Datasets for workflows that need their native grids, times, or depth levels.

Monthly aggregation of 8-day products uses an unweighted mean of samples assigned to each calendar month; it is not a day-overlap-weighted integration. Reindexed dates may be entirely missing for some variables. Source-wide MITHO summaries repeated along time should not be treated as independent monthly observations. Likewise, a maximum category in a coarser GeoZarr group represents the most severe contributing cell, rather than a class at every location in that block.

Open the store containing the variables you need, then select a region, time, and depth before computing. When comparing hourly, daily, and monthly values, aggregate them to a common time interval.

Create the new grid, select surface salinity (depth=0) and the careheat category data for the same day,  for the whole of the Med and copy the nearest source value to each target cell.

# 1. Define bounding box for the Mediterranean Sea
LON_MIN, LON_MAX = -6.0, 37.0   # From the Strait of Gibraltar to the Levantine coast
LAT_MIN, LAT_MAX = 30.0, 46.0   # From the North African coast to the northern Adriatic
TARGET_RESOLUTION_DEG = 1 / 12
TIME_TARGET = "2019-06-01"

# 2. Calculate the number of cells for longitude and latitude separately
n_cells_lon = int(round((LON_MAX - LON_MIN) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_DEG))
n_cells_lat = int(round((LAT_MAX - LAT_MIN) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_DEG))

# 3. Create 1D coordinate arrays (cell centers)
target_lon = LON_MIN + (np.arange(n_cells_lon) + 0.5) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_DEG
target_lat = LAT_MIN + (np.arange(n_cells_lat) + 0.5) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_DEG



source1 = source_dataset1[["sos"]].sel(
    time=slice(TIME_TARGET, TIME_TARGET), depth=0, drop=True,
    lon=slice(LON_MIN - 0.25, LON_MAX + 0.25),
    lat=slice(LAT_MIN - 0.25, LAT_MAX + 0.25),
)

source2 = source_dataset2[["category"]].sel(
    time=slice(TIME_TARGET, TIME_TARGET), drop=True,
    lon=slice(LON_MIN - 0.25, LON_MAX + 0.25),
    lat=slice(LAT_MIN - 0.25, LAT_MAX + 0.25),
)



sss = source1.interp(lon=target_lon, lat=target_lat, method="nearest")
caheat_cat = source2.interp(lon=target_lon, lat=target_lat, method="nearest")

# align the time coordinates
sss['time'] = caheat_cat['time']

cube = xr.merge([sss, caheat_cat])
cube = cube.rio.write_crs("EPSG:4326").rio.set_spatial_dims(x_dim="lon", y_dim="lat")
cube



fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=2, figsize=(10,5))
cube.sos.isel(time=0).plot(ax=ax[0])
cube.category.isel(time=0).plot(ax=ax[1])

records.content:
Use Dask to read the roughly 320 m overviews of the ESA WorldCover 2021 tiles in parallel, then merge them. Classes 0 (unmapped) and 80 (permanent water) are retained. Minimum resampling excludes a target cell if it contains mapped land; areas outside the mosaic remain retained. Unmapped areas are not confirmed water.

Apply the spatial mask to salinity across time and keep water_mask in the output (1 retained, 0 excluded).

left, bottom, right, top = cube.rio.bounds()
WC_BASE = "https://esa-worldcover.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com"
tiles = gpd.read_file(f"{WC_BASE}/v100/2020/esa_worldcover_2020_grid.geojson").cx[left:right, bottom:top]

@delayed
def read_worldcover_tile(tile):
    with rioxarray.open_rasterio(
        f"{WC_BASE}/v200/2021/map/ESA_WorldCover_10m_2021_v200_{tile}_Map.tif",
        overview_level=4, lock=False,
    ) as src:
        return src.load()

with ProgressBar():
    wc = merge_arrays(
        compute(*[read_worldcover_tile(tile) for tile in sorted(tiles.ll_tile)]),
        nodata=0,
    ).squeeze("band", drop=True)

water = wc.isin([0, 80]).astype("uint8").rio.write_nodata(255)
water_mask = water.rio.reproject_match(cube, resampling=Resampling.min, nodata=255)
water_mask = water_mask.where(water_mask != 255, 1)
water_mask = water_mask.rename({"x": "lon", "y": "lat"}).rename("water_mask")
cube["sos"] = cube.sos.where(water_mask == 1)
cube["water_mask"] = water_mask
cube.sos.isel(time=0).plot()

Run the examples in order: Parquet -> COG -> Zarr.

These notebooks show how to convert datasets into object-storage optimised formats and generate metadata for them. The focus is on file layout and metadata, not on deciding the scientifically correct reprojection or resampling method for every variable. Those choices remain dataset-specific.

The examples cover:

Format

Best for

Why it matters in object storage

Zarr

Multidimensional arrays such as time/depth/y/x cubes

Chunked reads let analysis load only the pieces it needs.

Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)

Single rasters or raster stacks exposed as files

Internal tiling and overviews enable efficient range reads and quicklooks.

GeoParquet

Vector geometries and tabular point data

Columnar storage, embedded geospatial metadata, and fast filtering.

For example datatype we also show how we genereated its associated metadata. Rich metadata ensures that the datasets are more accessible - 

https://esa-earthcode.github.io/documentation/Community and Best Practices/FAIR and Open Science Best Practices/Data.

All the metadata generated for the datasets and hosted on the Open Science Catalog is in STAC format. The SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) specification was designed to establish a standard, unified language to talk about geospatial data, allowing it to be more easily searchable and queryable. For more information and a introduction to STAC, see 

https://​esa​-earthcode​.github​.io​/tutorials​/stac​-and​-data​-access/ .

item

GeoParquet is a cloud-friendly way to store geospatial vector data, such as points, lines, and polygons, in 

Apache Parquet. It is useful when the data is fundamentally a table of features with geometry and attributes, rather than a raster image or a gridded data cube.

Parquet is a columnar storage format with broad support across data tools. GeoParquet builds on it by defining how geometry columns and geospatial metadata, such as the coordinate reference system (CRS), are stored. Because GeoParquet is still standard Parquet, general-purpose tools can read the table, while geospatial tools such as GeoPandas, GDAL, and QGIS can also interpret the geometry.

This page is adapted from the 

Cloud-Native Geospatial Guide, with examples from polar data access workflows.

Antarctic grounding lines are a natural vector dataset: each feature has a line geometry plus attributes such as date and sensor. The example below reads a GeoParquet file directly from object storage using GeoPandas.import geopandas as gpd

bucket = "s3://EarthCODE/"
endpoint_url = "https://s3.waw4-1.cloudferro.com"
region_name = "eu-west-2"
file = "OSCAssets/polar_cube_datasets/groundlines/InSAR_GL_Antarctica.parquet"

gdf = gpd.read_parquet(
    f"{bucket}{file}",
    storage_options={
        "anon": True,
        "client_kwargs": {
            "endpoint_url": endpoint_url,
            "region_name": region_name,
        },
    },
)

gdf.head()

Once loaded, the data behaves like a normal GeoDataFrame:gdf["SENSOR"].unique()

You can reproject and plot the geometries in Antarctic Polar Stereographic coordinates:import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 12))
gdf.to_crs("EPSG:3031").plot(column="SENSOR", legend=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Grounding-line observations by sensor")

The important pattern is simple: open the remote vector asset directly, inspect its attributes, and then filter, plot, or join it with other datasets.

Reading and writing GeoParquet has been 

supported in GDAL since version 3.5, so it can be used in software such as GeoPandas and QGIS.

Warning



In GeoPandas, use 

read_parquet and 

to_parquet to read and write GeoParquet. These are different from read_file and to_file, which are commonly used for formats such as Shapefile or GeoPackage.

Because GeoParquet stores geometries in standard 

Well-Known Binary (WKB), it supports the geometry types defined in the OGC Simple Features specification: Point, LineString, Polygon, MultiPoint, MultiLineString, MultiPolygon, and GeometryCollection.

Where possible, store a single geometry type per file. For example, a grounding-line dataset is easier to consume if all features are line geometries.

Parquet files are laid out differently from row-oriented formats like CSV or FlatGeobuf.

A Parquet file consists of a sequence of chunks called row groups. Each row group contains column chunks: contiguous blocks of values for each column. All row groups in the file share the same schema.

The file footer stores metadata describing the schema, the byte range of every column chunk, and optional column statistics such as minimum and maximum values. A reader usually fetches the footer first, then makes targeted reads for the columns and row groups needed by a query.

Because Parquet is internally chunked, readers can sometimes skip row groups that cannot match a filter. This works best when the file is sorted or partitioned by a useful field, such as year, sensor, basin, or region.

Note



Parquet is a file format, not a database. It supports efficient column reads and row-group skipping, but it does not replace a spatial database with multiple indexes. For complex spatial queries, use a database or a dedicated spatial indexing workflow.

Parquet is compressed internally by default. Compression tends to work well because values within a column are often similar to one another. A reader can fetch and decompress individual column chunks, although it cannot read partial data from inside a compressed chunk.

Spatial indexes are not yet part of the GeoParquet standard. For large spatial datasets, one common pattern is to split data into multiple GeoParquet files by region or tile and describe those files with 

STAC.

Small and medium vector products are often easiest to publish as a single .parquet file. Larger products may be split into multiple files, especially if they are produced by a distributed system or partitioned by a field such as year or region.

For multi-file datasets, a top-level metadata file such as _metadata can help readers avoid opening every individual Parquet footer before reading data. If new files are added later, keep the schema consistent and regenerate shared metadata when needed.

Some details of GeoParquet metadata in multi-file layouts are still evolving in the specification.
Parquet files are immutable. To modify or append data, write a new file or add another file to a partitioned dataset.

Parquet supports a rich type system, including nested types such as lists and maps. This makes it possible to store structured attributes alongside geometry, although simple scalar columns are usually easiest for broad interoperability.

records.content:
The target grid is defined from the projected source footprint. Coordinates are cell centres, and y is descending so raster outputs have a conventional north-up transform.

lat = ds["latitude"].values
lon = ds["longitude"].values
lon = ((lon + 180) % 360) - 180

transformer = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", TARGET_CRS, always_xy=True)
source_x, source_y = transformer.transform(lon, lat)

geo_mask = np.isfinite(source_x) & np.isfinite(source_y)
source_points = np.column_stack([source_x[geo_mask], source_y[geo_mask]])

xmin = np.floor(np.nanmin(source_x) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_M) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_M
xmax = np.ceil(np.nanmax(source_x) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_M) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_M
ymin = np.floor(np.nanmin(source_y) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_M) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_M
ymax = np.ceil(np.nanmax(source_y) / TARGET_RESOLUTION_M) * TARGET_RESOLUTION_M

x_grid = np.arange(xmin + TARGET_RESOLUTION_M / 2, xmax, TARGET_RESOLUTION_M)
y_grid = np.arange(ymax - TARGET_RESOLUTION_M / 2, ymin, -TARGET_RESOLUTION_M)
target_xx, target_yy = np.meshgrid(x_grid, y_grid)
target_points = np.column_stack([target_xx.ravel(), target_yy.ravel()])

print(f"Target grid: {len(x_grid)} columns x {len(y_grid)} rows at {TARGET_RESOLUTION_M} m")

records.content:
The KDTree lookup is computed once and reused for every depth slice. Missing source cells are written using a numeric nodata value because many GeoTIFF readers do not treat NaN consistently.

tree = cKDTree(source_points)
_, nearest_source_indices = tree.query(target_points, k=1)
nearest_source_indices = nearest_source_indices.reshape(target_xx.shape)





written_files = []
for depth_index, depth_value in zip(depth_indices, selected_depths):
    source_values = ds["Tice"].isel(depth=depth_index).values
    source_values = source_values[geo_mask]
    projected = source_values[nearest_source_indices].astype("float32")
    projected = np.where(np.isfinite(projected), projected, NODATA_VALUE).astype("float32")

    da = xr.DataArray(
        projected,
        dims=("y", "x"),
        coords={"y": y_grid, "x": x_grid},
        name="Tice",
        attrs={
            "long_name": "Ice sheet temperature",
            "units": ds["Tice"].attrs.get("units", "K"),
            "source_depth_m": float(depth_value),
            "reprojection_method": "nearest_source_point_after_projection",
        },
    )
    da = da.rio.write_crs(TARGET_CRS).rio.write_nodata(NODATA_VALUE)

    output_file = DATA_DIR / f"Tice_EPSG3031_depth_{int(round(float(depth_value)))}m.tif"
    da.rio.to_raster(
        output_file,
        driver="COG",
        compress="DEFLATE",
        blocksize=512,
        overview_resampling="nearest",
        BIGTIFF="IF_SAFER",
    )
    written_files.append(output_file)
    print(f"Wrote {output_file.name}")

import rioxarray

import cartopy.feature as cfeature

# 1. Define the path to your saved COG
cog_path = written_files[0]

# 2. Determine available overview levels dynamically using rasterio
with rasterio.open(cog_path) as src:
    # Get the list of downsampling factors (overviews) built into band 1
    overviews = src.overviews(1)
    num_overviews = len(overviews)

print(f"Total overview levels found: {num_overviews}")

# 3. Calculate First, Middle, and Last indices
# rioxarray uses 0-based indexing for overviews
first_level = 0
middle_level = num_overviews // 2
last_level = num_overviews - 1

levels_to_plot = [
    ("First (Highest Res Overview)", first_level),
    ("Middle Overview", middle_level),
    ("Last (Lowest Res Overview)", last_level)
]

# 4. Set up a 1x3 matplotlib figure with Cartopy projections
proj = ccrs.SouthPolarStereo()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6), subplot_kw={'projection': proj})

# 5. Loop through our chosen levels and axes
for ax, (title_label, level_idx) in zip(axes, levels_to_plot):
    
    # Load just this specific overview level into memory
    da_overview = rioxarray.open_rasterio(
        cog_path, 
        overview_level=level_idx, 
        masked=True
    ).sel(band=1)
    
    # Set up map extent and basemap features
    ax.set_extent([-180, 180, -90, -60], ccrs.PlateCarree())
    ax.add_feature(cfeature.LAND, facecolor='lightgray', zorder=0)
    ax.add_feature(cfeature.OCEAN, facecolor='aliceblue', zorder=0)
    ax.coastlines(resolution='50m', color='black', linewidth=1, zorder=2)
    ax.gridlines(draw_labels=True, color='gray', alpha=0.5, linestyle='--')
    
    # Plot the data onto the current axis
    da_overview.plot.pcolormesh(
        ax=ax,
        x='x',
        y='y',
        transform=proj,
        cmap='inferno',
        zorder=1, 
        cbar_kwargs={
            'orientation': 'horizontal',
            'shrink': 0.8,
            'label': 'Ice Temp (K)' if ax == axes[1] else '' # Only label middle colorbar to save space
        }
    )
    
    # Update the title with dynamic shape information
    shape_str = f"{da_overview.shape[0]}x{da_overview.shape[1]}"
    ax.set_title(f"{title_label}\nLevel: {level_idx} | Shape: {shape_str}", fontsize=12)

# 6. Add a main title and adjust layout
plt.suptitle("COG Pyramid Exploration: Resolution vs. Overview Level", fontsize=16, y=1.05)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
